The vast majority of patients going through Probably Genetic don’t pay out of pocket for their tests. (istock/gettyimagesplus/bymuratdeniz)
Probably Genetic, an AI platform powering the research, diagnosis and treatment of genetic diseases, has raised $12 million in series A funding, Fierce Healthcare has learned.

The round was led by Threshold, with participation from Y Combinator and other existing investors. The capital brings the company’s total to $14 million and will be used to grow the core part of the business, for hiring and to enter the drug discovery arena.

The company’s primary product is a physician-ordered genetic test for undiagnosed rare disease patients, who typically face a seven-year diagnostic odyssey before getting answers. There are two pathways to testing: free testing, through pharma partnerships, and insurance-billed testing. The free programs address specific conditions, with a limited number of tests available at a time.

Patients can check their eligibility by completing a health and diagnostic assessment online. Probably Genetic’s AI platform converts self-reported symptoms, medical records and biological data into phenotypic data that it hopes can be used to train AI models for precision medicine in the future. Thus far, it has collected data from 130,000 patients.

While today, Probably Genetic collects saliva samples for genetic testing, it plans to expand to proteomic testing in 2027, which requires blood draws. Proteomic sequencing data is crucial for drug discovery. This testing is not something patients would pay for, nor is it something that would be reimbursed through insurance. Instead, this will be paid for by pharma partners.

“We can already train AI models that can cut that diagnostic delay short, but to train those models, you need really good data—and the data to train these models doesn’t exist today,” Lukas Lange, Ph.D., co-founder and CEO, told Fierce Healthcare in an exclusive interview.

Probably Genetic does not have its own labs, working with half a dozen partners today to run the sequencing. It doesn’t see these other labs as its competition. “The biggest game here is actually not played on the diagnostic side, because unfortunately there is such a vast pool of patients out there that need to get diagnosed,” Lange said. “The competition is going to be in actual discovery.”

Most genetic diseases have no treatments. That’s why Probably Genetic hopes to enter the drug discovery arena. The ideal scenario, laid out by Lange, would get someone personalized preventive therapeutics based on their genetic testing, before they even experience symptoms of their illness.
Probably Genetic was founded in 2018 and is profitable. It claims to help diagnose over half of patients who previously had unexplained symptoms.
